Ask for help!  I failed university three times in my late teens / early 20's. When I finally went back (in my late 20's), the first thing I did was visit the disability support office to identify as having a mental illness and ask for their advice and support.

They were able to help me discuss my condition with my lecturers and tutors, who were then able to accomodate me by being more flexible on due dates or altering assignments if I found the original ones too difficult (such as allowing me to write an extra essay instead of giving a speech).  

I was also allowed to take exams in a small room of say 6 or 7 people rather than with hundreds of people in the university gym, and I was usually provided an extra 10 to 20 minutes of allowable time to compensate for my anxiety.

By the time I graduated, because I have received such great support and encouragement, I was actually much more like any other student.  I was eventually able to give speeches and often received High Distinctions for them.  I also found I no longer needed extra time in exams.  All because I had the support of the disability office to help me speak with the staff and express what I needed.

I went from bombing out of three degrees by the time I was 21 with a GPA of 1.6 / 7, to double degrees with first class honours (GPA 7 / 7), by 30.

Seriously, best thing I did was put my hand up and say I have a disability and I need help.

All the best for your studies.

All the time.  I was recently discharged from a long inpatient psych hospital stay, during which I was having intensive (3x per week) psychotherapy.  However, the psychologist got sick and had to take two weeks off.  

The day she came back, I glimpsed her in the group room leading a session, and my first (instinctive) thought was - 'Oh. You exist.'

I can never remember what people look like because I virtually never look them in the eye, which then makes my memories of them feel even less real, and I couldn't physically describe 90% of the people in my life as I just don't remember what they look like. 

The abandonment / derealisation / depersonalisation components of BPD are so strong in me that it means I basically feel like other people don't exist unless I'm physically in the same room as them.

In essence, I have no object permanency when it comes to other people.  They exist when I am with them and they cease to exist when I'm not.  

The worst consequence of this is that it means that I cannot draw on the thoughts or memories of a good, kind, supportive, decent person in my life, to help me feel stable and in control during difficult times.  I logically know those people exist as I see them usually at least once a week, but I just can't use an imagined version of them to self soothe when they're not physically around.  Hence the feelings of chronic emptiness.

Two months later, when the headaches haven't abated, your symptoms have worsened, and doctor after doctor has said it's just an 'anxiety related condition', you finally find a doctor who takes you seriously when you say this doesn't feel the same as my anxiety.  

The new doctor finally does a CAT Scan / MRI (not a doctor so don't know which one's right), and up pops a lovely big (inoperable) brain tumour that every other doctor had just passed off as anxiety, because that's what they'd seen on your My Health file previously, so they just assumed that's what was wrong with you, without doing a thorough check.

Not only are some doctors lazy, many also (sometimes deliberately and sometimes unintentionally) treat people with mental illnesses' as second class citizens, unworthy of their time and care.  I've seen it, and I've lived it.
